lines.cap: Your security clearance, part three: adjudication.
The investigation is done. Now someone decides. That's adjudication.
Step seven: adjudication. A DCSA adjudicator weighs your case against 13 national adjudicative guidelines, set out in Security Executive Agent Directive 4.
The 13 are: allegiance to the United States, foreign influence, foreign preference, sexual behavior, and personal conduct;
financial considerations, alcohol consumption, drug involvement and substance misuse, and psychological conditions;
criminal conduct, handling protected information, outside activities, and use of information technology.
Each guideline lists conditions that raise a concern, and conditions that can ease it.
You are looked at as a whole person. A single bad moment in time doesn't automatically mean a denial.
Adjudicators weigh how serious it was, how recent and how often, your age at the time, whether it was voluntary, and whether you've changed.
Time, honesty, and changed behavior can mitigate past issues.
But any real doubt is resolved in favor of national security.
Most cases end here, with a favorable decision. Some are approved with conditions and extra monitoring.
That's called conditional eligibility. DCSA can use it to monitor a concern through continuous vetting instead of starting due process.
If the adjudicator can't decide in your favor, the case goes to DOHA, the Defense Office of Hearings and Appeals.
If DOHA's attorneys agree there's a real concern, you receive a Statement of Reasons, or SOR, listing each one.
lines.say: If Doha's attorneys agree there's a real concern, you receive a Statement of Reasons, or S O R, listing each one.

lines.cap: If they don't agree, eligibility can still be granted.
Step nine: if you receive an SOR and want to pursue the clearance, you will need to respond.
lines.say: Step nine: if you receive an S O R and want to pursue the clearance, you will need to respond.

lines.cap: You have 20 days to answer in writing, under oath, admitting or denying each allegation.
You can choose: a hearing before an administrative judge, or a decision on the written record.
On the written record, you get a copy of the government's evidence and have 30 days to respond with your own documents and explanation.
At a hearing, a government attorney called Department Counsel presents the case. You can testify, call witnesses, and present documents.
You carry the burden of persuasion, so explain the circumstances and show what has changed.
You may bring a lawyer or a personal representative. If you don't respond at all, the clearance is denied.
Step ten: the judge decides. Either side can appeal to the DOHA Appeal Board within 15 days.
A final denial means waiting one year before your employer can apply again.
That's adjudication: the guidelines, the whole person, and due process if there are concerns.
Once you're approved, a clearance needs looking after. That's part four: maintenance.
